vignette:
Koa speaks of his grandmother with a reverence that makes the past feel present. He describes the scent of hibiscus and coconut oil that always clung to her, the way her hands, though wrinkled, were always steady when she'd weave palm fronds. She was the anchor of his family, the keeper of stories and recipes. He had just finished his pharmacy degree, the first in his family to do so, and the pride in her eyes was a memory he used to cherish. Now, it's a memory that burns.

The change began eight months ago, on a Tuesday. He'd stopped by her house after his shift at the community pharmacy, a routine he'd kept for years. He remembers the unsettling quiet, the front door slightly ajar. The memory, when it surfaces now, isn't a linear story but a series of sensory fragments that ambush him. It's the metallic tang of blood before he even saw her. It's the sight of her small frame crumpled at the bottom of the short staircase, a vibrant floral-print dress stained a dark, horrifying crimson. It's the cold, unforgiving tile against his knees as he fumbled for his phone, his pharmacist's mind racing through protocols and prognoses, all of it useless noise against the sheer panic. He remembers the gurgling sound she made when she tried to speak his name.

He rode in the ambulance, his white coat still on, a stark and ironic symbol of a healing profession that left him utterly helpless. In the sterile, fluorescent-lit hospital, he understood the doctors' hushed jargon all too well. Subdural hematoma. Uncontrolled bleeding, complicated by her blood thinners-the very same warfarin he dispensed to dozens of elderly patients every week. She never regained consciousness. She was gone by morning.

In the months since, Koa has constructed a life of careful avoidance. He works double shifts, volunteering for every holiday, finding a strange, punishing comfort in the pharmacy's sterile order. But the triggers are everywhere. An elderly woman who shuffles to the counter, her hand trembling as she takes her prescription, can send a jolt of ice through his veins. The sharp clang of a dropped pill bottle makes him flinch, his heart hammering against his ribs as if the sound were a gunshot. He'll be counting out oxycodone tablets, his fingers moving automatically, when the image of his grandmother on the floor will flash behind his eyes, so vivid he loses count and has to start again. His manager has commented on his fatigue, his uncharacteristic shortness with patients who ask too many questions.

Sleep offers little escape. He often jolts awake in the dark, heart pounding, the echo of that gurgling sound in his ears. He feels a gnawing guilt that has settled deep in his bones-he should have checked on her earlier, he should have insisted she move into a single-story home, he, the healthcare professional, should have somehow prevented it. This guilt has become a wall between him and his family. They want to grieve together, to share stories of her, but he just nods, his throat tight, unable to contribute. He hasn't been back to her house. He can't bring himself to smell the hibiscus that still blooms in her yard. He feels disconnected, as if he's watching his own life from a great distance, the vibrant colors of his world muted to gray. He is functioning, but he is not living.
